math-classical-ml: bias-variance
Explain the bias-variance trade-off. How do you tell which problem you have?

Bias is error from a model too simple to capture the pattern; variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to its training sample. High training error with similar validation error points to bias: add capacity or better features. Low training error with much higher validation error points to variance: add data, regularize, or simplify. Learning curves against training set size show which one you are facing.
l1-vs-l2
What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization, and when would you use each?

L2 penalizes squared weights and shrinks them smoothly, which works well when many features each contribute a little. L1 penalizes absolute weights, and its corner at zero pushes many weights to exactly zero, so it also selects features. Use L1 when you expect a sparse signal or want a small model. Elastic net combines both and handles correlated features better than L1 alone.
class-imbalance
Your fraud dataset is 0.1% positive. How do you train and evaluate the model?

Do not use accuracy, since predicting all negative scores 99.9%. Measure precision-recall AUC and recall at a precision the business accepts. Keep the validation set at the true rate. For training, use class weights or careful resampling on the training fold only. Tune the decision threshold from the cost of a miss against the cost of a false alarm, and calibrate probabilities if you resampled.
roc-vs-pr
When is PR-AUC more useful than ROC-AUC?

ROC-AUC uses the false positive rate, whose denominator is all negatives, so with heavy imbalance a large number of false positives barely moves it. PR-AUC uses precision, which directly shows what fraction of alerts are real. Use PR-AUC for rare-event problems. ROC-AUC is still useful for measuring ranking quality independent of class balance, and it can be compared across datasets with different base rates.
boosting-vs-bagging
How do bagging and boosting differ? Compare random forest with XGBoost.

Bagging trains deep, high-variance trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them, which mainly reduces variance. Boosting trains shallow trees in sequence, each fitting the errors of the ensemble so far, which mainly reduces bias. Random forest is robust and needs little tuning. XGBoost usually scores higher on tabular data but needs early stopping and tuning of learning rate and depth, and it can overfit noisy labels.
svm
How does an SVM work, and what does the kernel trick do?

An SVM finds the separating hyperplane with the largest margin, and only the points on or inside the margin, the support vectors, define it. The C parameter trades margin width against training errors. The kernel trick computes inner products as if data were mapped into a higher-dimensional space, without computing the mapping. Training cost grows quickly with rows, so SVMs are rarely chosen for very large datasets.
logistic-regression
Why does logistic regression use log loss rather than squared error?

With a sigmoid output, squared error gives a non-convex problem and very small gradients when the model is confidently wrong. Log loss is the negative log likelihood of a Bernoulli model, it is convex in the weights, and it penalizes confident mistakes heavily. Weights are read as changes in log odds, which is why the model stays popular when explanations matter. It needs scaled features for regularization to treat them fairly.
pca
What does PCA do, and when does it fail?

PCA finds orthogonal directions of highest variance using the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or equivalently the SVD of centered data. Keeping the top components compresses data while preserving most variance. Scale features first or large units dominate. It fails when the useful signal is not in the high-variance directions or when structure is non-linear, and the components are harder to explain than the original features.
kmeans
How does k-means work, what are its limits, and how do you choose k?

It alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to its cluster's mean, which reduces within-cluster squared distance but only reaches a local optimum, so use k-means++ and several restarts. It assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters and is sensitive to scale and outliers. Choose k with the silhouette score, the elbow method, and above all whether the clusters are useful for the task.
trees-splits
How does a decision tree choose a split, and why do trees overfit?

At each node it tries candidate splits and picks the one with the largest reduction in impurity, using Gini or entropy for classification and variance for regression. Greedy splitting can continue until each leaf is nearly pure, which memorizes noise. Control this with maximum depth, minimum samples per leaf and pruning, or by averaging many trees. Trees need no feature scaling and handle non-linear interactions naturally.
feature-engineering
How do you approach feature engineering for a tabular model?

Start from what would be known at prediction time, since anything later is leakage. Use domain ratios, time-window aggregates and recency features. Encode high-cardinality categoricals with target encoding fitted inside folds, or hashing. Treat missingness as a possible signal. Scale only for models that need it. Add features one group at a time, keep those that improve validation, and check that serving can compute each one within its latency budget.
missing-data
How do you handle missing values? When is dropping rows wrong?

First ask why values are missing. If missingness depends on the outcome or on other features, dropping rows biases the model and serving will still see missing values. Options are median or model-based imputation with a missing indicator, or tree models that handle missing values natively. Fit imputers on training data only. Also confirm production has the same missing pattern, since a broken pipeline can look like missing data.
ab-testing
Design an A/B test for a new ranking model. What can go wrong?

Choose one primary metric and guardrails such as latency. Fix the minimum detectable effect, then compute sample size from baseline variance, power and significance before starting. Randomize by user, not request, and run full weekly cycles. Problems include peeking at results, novelty effects, sample ratio mismatch, interference between users, and testing many metrics. A sample ratio check should run first, because it can invalidate the entire result.
p-values
What does a p-value actually mean, and what is a common misreading?

It is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it says nothing about effect size. With very large samples, tiny useless effects become significant, so report a confidence interval and judge practical impact. Running many tests inflates false positives, so correct for multiple comparisons.
causal-vs-correlation
A feature strongly predicts churn. Can you tell the business that changing it will reduce churn?

No. Prediction shows association, which may come from a confounder or reverse causation. For example, support tickets may predict churn because unhappy users file them, and reducing tickets would not fix the cause. To estimate an effect, run an experiment. If you cannot, use methods such as difference-in-differences or propensity matching, and state their assumptions. Uplift models target who responds to an action rather than who is at risk.
time-series-validation
Why can't you use random k-fold on a time series, and how do you validate instead?

Random folds let the model train on the future and predict the past, and nearby points are correlated, so the score is too optimistic. Use rolling or expanding-window validation, with a gap between train and test when features use lag windows. Compare against naive baselines such as last value or seasonal last value. Report error by horizon, because accuracy usually falls the further ahead you predict.
calibration
What is model calibration and when does it matter?

A model is calibrated if, among predictions of 0.8, about 80% are positive. Good ranking does not guarantee this, and boosted trees and deep networks are often miscalibrated. It matters when probabilities drive decisions, such as expected-cost thresholds, ad bidding or combining scores. Check with a reliability diagram and expected calibration error. Fix with Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling, fitted on a separate holdout.
deep-learning: vanishing-gradients
What causes vanishing and exploding gradients, and how are they fixed?

Backpropagation multiplies many Jacobians, so gradients shrink or grow exponentially with depth. Saturating activations such as sigmoid make shrinkage worse. Fixes include ReLU-family activations, careful initialization such as He or Xavier, normalization layers, and residual connections, which give gradients a direct path. Gradient clipping handles explosions, especially in RNNs. Check by logging per-layer gradient norms during training.
rnn-lstm
Why do LSTMs handle long sequences better than plain RNNs, and why did transformers replace them?

A plain RNN multiplies through the same transition at each step, so gradients vanish. An LSTM adds a cell state with gated, mostly additive updates, so information and gradients persist longer. GRUs simplify this with fewer gates. Transformers replaced them because attention connects any two positions in one step and allows parallel training, whereas RNNs must process tokens in order. LSTMs can still suit small streaming models.
cnn-properties
Why do CNNs work so well for images? Explain convolution and pooling.

Convolution applies the same small filter everywhere, so it uses few parameters and detects a pattern wherever it appears. Stacking layers grows the receptive field from edges to parts to objects. Pooling or strided convolution reduces resolution and adds tolerance to small shifts. These built-in assumptions let CNNs learn well from limited data, while vision transformers typically need more data or strong pretraining.
resnet
What problem do residual connections solve?

Very deep plain networks trained worse than shallower ones, even on training data, so it was an optimization problem rather than overfitting. A residual block learns a change added to its input, so doing nothing is easy, and identity shortcuts give gradients a clean path. This made networks with over a hundred layers trainable. The same idea appears in the add-and-norm structure of transformers.
batchnorm-vs-layernorm
Compare batch normalization and layer normalization. Why do transformers use layer norm?

Batch norm normalizes each feature across the batch and keeps running statistics for inference, so it depends on batch size and can behave differently between training and serving. Layer norm normalizes across features within each example, so it works with any batch size and variable sequence lengths. That makes it the natural choice for transformers. Batch norm remains effective for CNNs with reasonably large batches.
optimizers
Compare SGD with momentum, Adam and AdamW. What would you start with?

Momentum averages past gradients to speed progress along consistent directions. Adam also adapts a per-parameter step using squared gradient history, so it converges quickly with less tuning. AdamW applies weight decay directly to weights rather than through the gradient, which fixes how Adam interacts with L2. I would start with AdamW and warmup for transformers. SGD with momentum and a schedule can still generalize well for vision.
dropout
How does dropout work, and how does it behave at inference?

During training it zeroes each unit with probability p, which stops units relying on each other and acts like training many thinned networks. Common implementations scale the kept activations by 1/(1-p) so expected values match, then disable dropout at inference. Forgetting eval mode is a common bug that makes predictions noisy. Keeping dropout on at inference, Monte Carlo dropout, gives a rough uncertainty estimate.
cross-entropy-softmax
Why do we pair softmax with cross-entropy, and how should you compute it safely?

Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution, and cross-entropy is its negative log likelihood. Together they give a simple gradient, predicted probability minus target, times the input features at the last layer, and it stays large when the model is confidently wrong. Compute the loss directly from logits using a log-softmax function, because computing softmax first and then a log can underflow and produce infinities or NaNs.
loss-debugging
Training loss is NaN after a few hundred steps. How do you debug it?

Find the first bad step and log the loss, gradient norms and activation ranges. Common causes are a learning rate that is too high, log of zero, division by zero, bad input values, and FP16 overflow. Check the data for NaNs first, then lower the learning rate and add gradient clipping. Overfit one small batch to separate model bugs from data problems. PyTorch anomaly detection can locate the failing operation.
distributed-training
How does distributed data parallel training work, and what limits it?

Each GPU holds a model copy and processes a different slice of the batch. After backward, gradients are averaged with all-reduce so all copies stay identical. Limits are communication cost, slow stragglers and data loading bottlenecks. Larger effective batches usually need learning rate scaling with warmup. Models too large for one GPU need sharding methods such as FSDP or ZeRO, and long runs need checkpoint recovery.
mixed-precision
What is mixed-precision training and what can go wrong?

It runs most operations in FP16 or BF16 and keeps sensitive parts in FP32, saving memory and increasing speed. FP16 has a small range, so small gradients can underflow to zero; a loss scaler multiplies the loss to prevent this and skips steps that overflow. BF16 has the same range as FP32 with less precision, so it usually needs no scaler. Watch for NaNs and check accuracy against a full precision baseline.
gans
How do GANs train, and why did diffusion models overtake them?

A generator tries to fool a discriminator while the discriminator learns to separate real from fake, forming a minimax game. Training can be unstable, and mode collapse leaves the generator producing little variety. Diffusion models learn to reverse gradual noising with a simple regression loss, which is stable and covers modes better. Their cost is many sampling steps, though GANs and fast samplers remain useful when speed matters.
vae
What does a VAE optimize, and how does the reparameterization trick help?

A VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound, made of a reconstruction term and a KL term that keeps the latent distribution near a prior. Sampling is not differentiable, so the trick writes the latent as the mean plus the standard deviation times independent noise, which lets gradients flow to both. Too much KL weight can make the decoder ignore the latent, which is known as posterior collapse.
transfer-learning
With only 2,000 labelled images, how would you build a classifier?

Start with a pretrained backbone, freeze it, and train a new head. Then unfreeze the top layers at a lower learning rate if validation improves. Use strong augmentation and a split that prevents near-duplicate leakage. Check class balance and label quality, since label errors matter more with small data. Compare against simple features plus logistic regression, and consider active learning to spend further labelling budget where it helps most.
transformers: bert-vs-gpt
What is the difference between BERT and GPT?

BERT uses an encoder with bidirectional attention, so each token sees context on both sides, and it is trained by masking tokens. That suits classification and embeddings. GPT uses a decoder with causal masking, so each token sees only earlier ones, and it is trained to predict the next token, which suits generation. BERT cannot generate naturally, and GPT cannot use future context when representing a token.
why-sqrt-dk
Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by the square root of d_k?

If query and key components have variance one, their dot product has variance d_k, so larger dimensions produce larger scores. Large scores push softmax into a nearly one-hot region where gradients become very small. Dividing by the square root of d_k brings the variance back to about one, which keeps attention trainable. It is a simple variance correction, the same reasoning behind careful weight initialization.
multi-head
Why use multiple attention heads instead of one big head?

Each head projects into its own smaller subspace, so heads can learn different relationships, such as nearby syntax or long-range references. A single head averages everything into one attention pattern. The total cost stays about the same because each head's dimension is the model dimension divided by the number of heads. In practice, heads are not cleanly interpretable, and the benefit is mainly representational flexibility.
encoder-decoder-attention
Explain self-attention, cross-attention and causal masking.

In self-attention, queries, keys and values come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, queries come from the decoder and keys and values come from the encoder, which lets a translation model look at the source. Causal masking blocks attention to future positions during training, so the model cannot see the token it must predict. Decoder-only LLMs use masked self-attention and no cross-attention.
attention-complexity
What is the time and memory cost of attention, and how do models manage it?

Standard attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of sequence length. During generation, the KV cache avoids recomputing past keys and values, though its memory grows linearly with length. Methods include sliding windows, sparse attention, grouped-query attention to share keys and values across heads, and efficient kernels such as FlashAttention, which reduces memory traffic but computes exact attention.
temperature-top-p
Explain temperature, top-k and top-p sampling. How would you set them?

Temperature divides logits before softmax, so low values sharpen the distribution and high values flatten it. Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens, while top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability reaches p, adapting to how confident the model is. For extraction or code, use a low temperature. For creative work, use moderate temperature with top-p near 0.9. Evaluate settings on your task instead of relying on defaults.
llm-training-pipeline
Walk me through how an LLM such as Llama is trained, from data to a chat model.

Pretraining optimizes next-token cross-entropy over huge cleaned and deduplicated text, using distributed GPUs, mixed precision and checkpointing. That produces a text completer. Post-training then teaches behaviour through supervised fine-tuning on instruction data, followed by preference optimization such as RLHF or DPO, plus safety training. Evaluation runs throughout on held-out benchmarks and red teaming. Finally, the model is quantized and optimized for serving.
context-window
What happens when a prompt exceeds the context window, and how do you design for it?

The API rejects it or truncates it, often removing something important without warning. Design a budget: count tokens before sending and reserve room for output. Keep system instructions and recent turns, summarize older history, and retrieve only relevant documents. For long documents, use map-reduce or hierarchical summarization. Prompt order also matters, since stable prefixes benefit from caching and long context can reduce quality even when it fits.
production-mlops: feature-store
What is a feature store, and what problem does it solve?

It keeps feature definitions in one place, with an offline store for training and a low-latency online store for serving. The main problem it solves is training-serving skew, where the two paths compute a feature differently. Point-in-time joins also prevent leakage from future values. It adds real infrastructure cost, so a small team with few real-time features may not need one until features are reused widely.
training-serving-skew
Offline AUC is 0.92 but production performance is poor. How do you investigate?

First compare logged production features with what the offline pipeline computes for the same requests, since skew is the most common cause. Check for leakage in training, time-based shift, and whether the offline split matched production. Confirm preprocessing and model version match. Then check label delay, and whether the model's own decisions change the data it sees. Shadow-mode logging would catch many of these before launch.
drift-types
Explain data drift and concept drift. How do you monitor when labels are delayed?

Data drift is a change in input distribution; concept drift is a change in the relationship between input and label. Without labels, monitor feature distributions using PSI or KS tests, prediction distributions, missing rates and proxy signals such as click-through. Drift alerts are noisy, so weight them by feature importance and business impact. When labels arrive, measure actual performance by cohort and use that to trigger retraining.
deployment-strategies
Compare shadow, canary and blue-green deployment for an ML model.

Shadow runs the new model on real traffic without affecting users, which is safe for latency and prediction checks but can't measure user impact. Canary sends a small share of real traffic to it and expands if metrics hold. Blue-green keeps two full environments for instant switching. A good sequence is shadow, then canary, then an A/B test for impact, with an automatic rollback path throughout.
retraining-strategy
How do you decide when to retrain a model?

Use the cost of decay. Measure how quickly performance falls by backtesting older models on newer data. Then choose a schedule or a trigger based on actual performance or drift. Each retrain should pass automated checks on data quality, a fixed test set and comparison with the current model. Retraining is not always the fix, since a broken pipeline would just train on bad data, so diagnose first.
reproducibility
How do you make model training reproducible?

Version code, data and configuration together, and record them with each model, using tools such as Git, DVC and MLflow. Pin dependencies in a container and log seeds and hardware. Full bit-level determinism on GPUs is costly and rarely needed, so aim to reproduce results within a small tolerance. Save the exact train and test splits, and a model registry should link every deployed model back to its run.
model-registry-rollback
A new model degrades conversion by 3% in production. What do you do in the first hour?

Roll back first, then investigate. Confirm the drop with guardrail metrics and rule out other releases or a data outage. A registry and versioned serving should make rollback a single quick action. Then preserve logs, compare the affected segments, and replay requests against both models. Afterwards, write a blameless review and add the missing check, such as a smaller canary or a segment-level alert.
kubernetes-gpu
How would you serve an LLM on Kubernetes, and how do you autoscale it?

Run each model server as a GPU pod with resource limits, with readiness probes that wait until the model has loaded. CPU-based autoscaling is misleading here, so scale on queue depth, active requests or GPU cache use. Cold starts take minutes, so keep warm spare capacity and pre-cache weights on nodes. Use a gateway for routing and rate limits, and allow in-flight streams to drain before removing a pod.
data-quality
How do you stop bad data from breaking a production model?

Validate at pipeline boundaries: schema, ranges, null rates, row counts, freshness and distributions, using tools such as Great Expectations or TFX Data Validation. Fail closed for training so a bad batch cannot produce a bad model. For serving, fall back to safe defaults and raise an alert. Assign owners to upstream data contracts, because most incidents begin with an upstream change that nobody announced.
system-design: recommender
Design a recommendation system for a video platform with 100 million users.

Clarify the goal, such as long-term watch time rather than clicks. Use stages: candidate generation with a two-tower model and approximate nearest neighbours, ranking with a deep model on rich features, then re-ranking for diversity and freshness. Serve within about 200 ms with a feature store. Handle cold start using content features and exploration. Log impressions to reduce feedback loops, evaluate offline with NDCG, and launch using A/B tests.
two-tower
Explain the two-tower retrieval model and how you would train and serve it.

One tower embeds the user and another embeds the item, and their dot product scores relevance. Train with positive interactions and sampled negatives, correcting for popular items being oversampled. Item embeddings are computed offline and stored in an ANN index, and the user embedding is computed at request time. Because the towers meet only at the end, feature crosses are limited, so a heavier ranking model follows.
search-ranking
Design ranking for e-commerce search.

Retrieve with both BM25 and embeddings to capture exact and semantic matches, then merge. Rank with learning-to-rank, such as LambdaMART or a deep model, using query, product and behaviour features. Clicks are biased by position, so correct for that in training. Measure NDCG offline and conversion online. Handle query understanding, spelling and zero-result queries, and add business rules for stock and policy after ranking.
fraud-system
Design a real-time payment fraud system with a 100 ms budget.

Separate a fast path from slower investigation. Combine rules with a gradient-boosted model using velocity features from a streaming pipeline, and precompute what you can. Labels arrive weeks later through chargebacks, so handle delay carefully. Fraudsters adapt, so monitor drift and retrain often. Choose thresholds from costs, with allow, review and block outcomes. Fail safely if the model is unavailable, and log reasons for review and compliance.
ads-ctr
Design a click-through rate prediction system for ads.

The score enters an auction as expected value, so calibration matters as much as ranking. Use features for user, ad and context, with hashing or embeddings for high-cardinality IDs, and a model such as DCN or DeepFM. Train continuously because ads change quickly. Watch for delayed conversions, sampling corrections and feedback loops. Measure log loss and calibration offline, then revenue and user experience in experiments.
enterprise-rag-design
Design an internal AI assistant over 10 million company documents with access control.

Ingest through connectors, parse with layout awareness, chunk, and embed. Store permissions with each chunk and filter at query time, never after generation. Use hybrid retrieval and reranking, then generate with citations and allow it to decline. Evaluate on a golden set from real users, tracking retrieval recall and faithfulness. Handle document updates and deletions incrementally, cache common queries, and audit access, because a permissions leak is the worst failure.
llm-gateway
Design a platform that serves LLMs for 50 internal teams.

Put a gateway in front that handles authentication, per-team quotas, routing, logging and cost attribution. Route by need, with small models for simple work and fallback when a provider fails. Add a semantic or prefix cache where it is safe. Separate interactive and batch traffic so batch work can't hurt latency. Provide shared evaluation and guardrails, version prompts, and redact personal data in logs.
llm-cost-estimate
Estimate the GPU cost of serving 1,000 requests per second with an LLM.

State assumptions: 1,000 input and 200 output tokens per request gives 200,000 output tokens per second. If one GPU sustains about 2,000 output tokens per second under the latency target, that needs about 100 GPUs, plus headroom for peaks and failures, so about 130. At $2 per GPU-hour that is $260 per hour, or about $190,000 a month. Measure real throughput, then reduce cost using caching and routing.
computer-vision-system
Design a visual defect detection system for a factory line.

Start with the cost of a missed defect against a false reject, and line speed, which sets the latency limit. Control lighting and camera setup first, since this often helps more than the model. Defects are rare, so use anomaly detection or heavy augmentation with a detector. Run on an edge device, send uncertain images to people, and feed reviews back into training. Monitor for changes in products, lighting and cameras.
multi-tenant-llm-isolation
How do you prevent one customer's data from leaking to another in a multi-tenant AI product?

Enforce tenant identity at every layer, from the authenticated request down to retrieval filters and cache keys, and never let the model make access decisions. Separate indexes for sensitive tenants. Scope prompt caches and logs by tenant. Treat retrieved text as untrusted, since it may contain injection. Keep training data opt-in. Test with cross-tenant probes in CI and audit all access, because prevention needs to be testable.
evaluation: Your model improves offline metrics but loses the A/B test. Why might this happen?

The offline metric may not represent the business goal, for example clicks instead of retention. Logged data reflects the old model's choices, so it hides what the new one would show. Other causes are training-serving skew, higher latency, novelty effects and a real effect in one segment hiding losses in another. Investigate by segment, check the experiment's validity, and find an offline metric that tracks online results.
How do you stop a prompt change from silently breaking an LLM feature?

Treat prompts as code: version them and run an evaluation set in CI on every change. Build the set from real traffic and past failures, with deterministic checks where possible and rubric-based LLM judges elsewhere. Run several samples, because output varies. Compare against the baseline with a clear pass threshold. After release, use a canary and online metrics, and add each new failure to the set.
How do you check whether a model is fair, and what trade-offs arise?

Measure performance by relevant group, including error rates, calibration and selection rates. Definitions can conflict: when base rates differ, you generally can't have both equal calibration and equal error rates. So choose with the people affected and with legal input. Removing a sensitive attribute doesn't remove proxies. Options include better data, reweighting, group-aware thresholds where permitted, and human review of high-stakes decisions.
How would you explain a model's decision to a regulator or a customer?

Choose by audience and risk. For high-stakes use, consider an inherently interpretable model. SHAP gives per-feature contributions for tree models, and a customer needs a plain reason plus what could change the result. Explanations describe the model, not causation, and correlated features can make them unstable. Keep model and data versions, so any past decision can be reproduced and audited.
safety: How do you build an LLM feature that handles personal data, in line with GDPR?

Minimize first: send only what the task needs, and detect and redact personal data before logs and third-party calls. Establish a legal basis and purpose, set retention limits, and support deletion across logs, indexes and training sets. Check where the provider stores data and whether it trains on it. Use on-device or private hosting for sensitive data. Run a privacy impact assessment, and don't put personal data in eval sets by default.
multimodal: Compare one-stage and two-stage object detectors. What is non-maximum suppression?

Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN propose regions and then classify them, which is often more accurate but slower. One-stage detectors such as YOLO predict boxes and classes in one pass, which suits real-time use. Non-maximum suppression removes overlapping duplicates by keeping the highest-scoring box and dropping others above an IoU threshold. DETR-style models predict a set directly and avoid it. Measure with mAP.
How do diffusion models generate images?

Training adds Gaussian noise to images in steps, and a U-Net or transformer learns to predict that noise at each level. Generation begins from pure noise and repeatedly removes the predicted noise. Latent diffusion works in a compressed VAE space to reduce cost. Text conditioning uses cross-attention, and classifier-free guidance strengthens it by mixing conditional and unconditional predictions. Faster samplers such as DDIM reduce the number of steps.
Design a real-time voice assistant. Where does the latency go?

The pipeline has voice activity detection, speech-to-text, the LLM and text-to-speech, and users notice delays above about a second. Stream everything: partial transcripts, LLM tokens, and speech sentence by sentence, so first audio begins early. Endpointing is a key trade-off, because waiting longer avoids cutting people off but adds delay. Support barge-in with echo cancellation. Measure time to first audio, not just total time.
coding: Implement k-means from scratch in NumPy. What would you test?

Initialize k centroids, preferably using k-means++. Loop: compute distances with broadcasting, assign each point to its nearest centroid, recompute means, and stop when assignments stop changing or at a maximum iteration count. Handle empty clusters by reseeding them. Test with clearly separated synthetic blobs, k equal to one, a fixed seed, and a check that within-cluster error never increases between iterations.
Implement scaled dot-product attention in PyTorch and explain the tensor shapes.

Given Q, K and V with shape batch, length, dim: scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k). Apply the mask by filling blocked scores with negative infinity before softmax on the last dimension, then return weights @ V. Output shape matches V's. For multi-head, reshape to batch, heads, length, head dim. Common bugs are masking after softmax and applying softmax to the wrong dimension.
Write precision, recall and F1 from scratch, and handle the edge cases.

Count true positives, false positives and false negatives. Precision is TP over TP plus FP, recall is TP over TP plus FN, and F1 is their harmonic mean. Guard every division against zero, and state the convention you use, usually returning zero. For multi-class work, explain macro averaging, which treats classes equally, against micro averaging, which treats examples equally. Test with all-negative predictions and no positive labels.
Find the top k most frequent items in a very large stream. What is your approach?

If it fits in memory, count with a hash map and keep a min-heap of size k, which takes O(n log k) time. If it doesn't, use an approximate sketch such as Count-Min with a heap, or Misra-Gries, which accept a bounded error for fixed memory. On a cluster, count by key with map-reduce, then merge. State your accuracy needs first, since they determine the design.
An interviewer gives you a coding problem you haven't seen. How do you work through it?

Restate it and ask about input size and edge cases. Give the brute-force solution and its complexity, then improve it. Most problems at ML roles use hash maps, two pointers, sliding windows, heaps, binary search, BFS or DFS, and basic dynamic programming. Talk as you work, write clean code, then test with a small example and an edge case. A working simple solution beats an unfinished clever one.
Using SQL, find each user's most recent purchase and their 7-day rolling spend.

Use window functions. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchased_at DESC) and filter to row 1 gives the latest purchase. For rolling spend, aggregate to one row per user per day, then use SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Days with no purchases need a calendar join, or the seven rows will span more than seven days.
behavioral: project-deep-dive
Walk me through the most impactful ML project you led.

Use a clear shape: the business problem and metric, the baseline, your role, key decisions and alternatives you rejected, what failed, and the measured outcome. Senior interviewers will probe, so know your data size, latency, cost, evaluation method and what you would change now. Say I for your own decisions and we for the team's. Prepare one project deeply enough to discuss for 30 minutes.
ml-not-needed
Tell me about a time you decided not to use ML, or to use a simpler model.

Show judgment. Describe the problem, then how you compared a simple rule or baseline with a complex model on accuracy, cost, latency and maintenance. Give numbers, such as a rules system reaching most of the value in two weeks. Explain how you convinced people who wanted something more advanced, and what would have changed your decision. Interviewers look for evidence over enthusiasm for technology.
failed-model
Tell me about a model that failed in production. What did you do?

Pick a real failure with consequences. Explain how it was detected, how you limited the damage, the root cause and the lasting fix, such as a new monitor or release check. Take ownership without blaming others. A blameless account that produced a system change is much stronger than a story with no mistakes. Quantify the impact, and say what you now do differently.
influence-stakeholders
How do you handle a product manager who wants a launch date your model can't safely meet?

Translate risk into business terms and bring options, not just a no. For example, offer a limited launch to low-risk users, a human review step, or a simpler first version, each with its risk and timeline. Agree a metric that defines ready. If leadership accepts a risk, record the decision and set monitoring and rollback. Seniors are judged on keeping trust while finding a way forward.
mentoring-technical-direction
As a senior engineer, how do you raise the quality of your team's ML work?

Give concrete examples, such as introducing design reviews for experiments, a shared evaluation harness, or standard launch checklists. Mentor by asking questions and pairing on hard problems, then let others own the result. Measure the effect, such as fewer incidents or faster iteration. Show you choose the highest-leverage work, including saying no, and that other people's growth counts as your output.
ambiguous-problem
You are told to use AI to reduce support costs, with no further detail. What do you do?

Clarify first: how much is spent now, which ticket types drive it, and what quality is acceptable. Analyse the data before choosing a method. Propose a small test, such as drafting replies for one common category with human review, and define success and guardrails. Compare build and buy, and estimate cost per ticket. Then scale what works. Interviewers want structured thinking, not an immediate architecture.
salary-senior-signals
What separates a senior ML engineer from a mid-level one in interviews?

Seniors start with the business problem and metric, state assumptions, and compare options with numbers instead of naming tools. They discuss failure modes, cost, monitoring and rollback without being asked. They know their past projects in depth, admit what they don't know, and explain trade-offs clearly. They also show ownership beyond code, such as influencing direction, handling ambiguity and helping others improve.
